answer: Yes. When you create a TOM with add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. The add form takes required-type (CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP, SFPPLUS) plus optional required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (true/false, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; only applicable to TOMs on the CHM7 card). Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show tom-type-<tom-type> and read the support-third-party-toms attribute, which states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to supported Nokia TOMs; its values are true and false. The same command also returns description (string 0..255), tom-type (identityref), data-rate (uint16, Gbps) and generic-subtype, the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. show tom-type with no key lists all supported TOM types. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) is used to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It appears under unprovisioned-inventory, which lists detected inventory that has not yet been accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. Use show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>. The slot-name is empty when the equipment is the chassis itself. Available attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, see set-time), and detection-timestamp, the last time the unprovisioned equipment was detected by the Node Controller. chassis-serial-number and slot-name are strings of length 0..16. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]; show usb with no key lists all USB ports on the node. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations (string, length 0..32). available-space is the current free storage space and total-space the total storage space in that file-system, both uint16 in MB. These three attributes apply only when type is storage; the other type value is power-supply, a port used to power external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the USB connector is inserted. Example: show usb-1-5-U1. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated (see take-snapshot). db-instance names the database snapshot to activate and defaults to temp. paraphrase is a short description of the database to be activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override is an action to override the sanity check, with values true and false and a default of false. The command runs in Operational mode. Examples: activate-snapshot sanity-check-override, and activate-snapshot onehour to activate a snapshot named onehour.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after enable-advanced-parameters on the optical carrier is set to true. Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, show advanced-parameter reports ERROR: object does not exist; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value, the configuration is not rejected, but show advanced-parameter reports the failed status for it. The commands are add/set/show/delete advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, default unknown. advanced-parameter-name is a string of length 0..256. Supported names, values and defaults for CHM6 and CHM7/7X are in the 1830 GX System Description Guide.

Use apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*]). For SerDes, template-type is serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; serdes-template is also the default template-type. If no specific TOMs are provided, that is the applicable-tom list is empty, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: apply-template serdes-template applies to everything, while apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1 targets that one TOM; multiple TOMs are comma separated. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm it with commit persist and abandon it with commit cancel. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit, all of these commands require the -id parameter, which defines the ID shared by commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel. All of these must be done in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with configure. commit -m=<message> attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use show config, and to get it back as replayable CLI, pipe it: show config | display commands, storing the result for later usage. This is the documented way to create a CLI script that can be used to restore the system configuration; see the display command for details. show config displays the system configuration and skips configurations that have their default values, so only non-default configuration is shown. The output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow it, supply an entity-id (instance ID of one entity) or an entity-type when all entities of a given type are relevant: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)].

It depends on the target you pick. configure <target> takes exclusive or shared, and the default is exclusive. In exclusive mode only this session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can make changes to the candidate configuration. The command moves you from operational mode into Candidate Configuration mode and is issued from Operational mode. You can also control how the candidate datastore is initialized: by default it starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; from-default starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; from-script=<script> imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands, replacing the running configuration content; from-commit=<commit-id> initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive.

Use show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]. This command shows the current values of the advanced parameters which are running on the system, as opposed to what you configured with add/set advanced-parameter. show current-advanced-parameter with no key lists them all, and a wildcard restricts to one carrier, for example show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*. Attributes are optical-carrier-name, current-advanced-parameter-name and value, all strings. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The running value can legitimately differ from the configured one. Note that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified; it is to be supported in a future release.

No. clear database performs a full wipe of the database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data; use the clear system command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Syntax: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>, where -f forces the command without confirmation. clear-type is full (default, reset to factory defaults), keep-networking (wipe but keep network configurations) or initialize-from-script (wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script, default directory /storage/scripts). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Transient alarms after the controller card reboot should be ignored.

Use db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>, where type defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption. To add integrity protection on top of encryption, run db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity; this enables the integrity check for the system database and will automatically reboot the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The command runs in Operational Mode. Verify the result with show db-protection-scheme, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and states that it can be changed via the db-migrate RPC; with integrity enabled, integrity-algorithm becomes hmac-sha2-512 rather than none.

Use show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode] and read integrity-status, which indicates the status of the integrity check with the values passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup and disabled. The same output shows encryption-algorithm, whose value is xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm with values hmac-sha2-512 or none, and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. A node with no integrity protection shows integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled and mode encryption-only. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use diff [-t|-c] candidate, run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore configuration and the current system configuration, covering created, deleted and changed objects, and shows only configurable attributes; new data means the candidate configuration and old data means the current system configuration. The default output is normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values. The -t flag presents the data as a side-by-side diff in a table. The -c flag presents it as CLI commands that would perform the same configuration as was done in the candidate datastore, which is the form you want as commands; -d gives the list of commands being executed. There is also diff commit <id> [<id>] to compare a commit-record against the running configuration or another commit-record, available when commit-records exist (commit-tracking enabled in system-policies) or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run discard-changes. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care and only enable one you understand. Using it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side, and the name must match a name known by the system. The commands are add extended-config-<name>, delete extended-config-<name> and show extended-config-<name> [description]. name is a string of length 0..64. The description attribute (string 0..255) displays the description of the extended-config provided by the system and its effect in the system, so read that before adding one. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Check the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> and read the service-impact attribute, which identifies whether applying this parameter change causes service impact; its values are service-affecting and non-service-affecting. If it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations. The companion attribute configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change, with values no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change and full-config-no-pll-change. The same command returns description, type, supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity, the number of values you must enter for the parameter. All attributes are read-only. Examples: show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/* or show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation.

Run lock. It locks database access to the current session and grants exclusive write access to that CLI session; it is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, another session, CLI or other type, that tries to make a configuration will receive an error. A lock will not be possible if another session is currently holding the lock. The lock is released by using the unlock command, or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or via inactivity time-out. Syntax is lock [-h], where -h displays help; there are no other parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode.

A named-value-set is addressed by a two-part key: named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a single value attribute, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The supported operations are add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>], set with the same form to change it, show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value] to read it, and delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

It can, and by default it does. set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value> controls this, with values disabled, auto-restore and auto-in-service, and the default is auto-in-service. With disabled, chassis storage is not used for restoration in this NE. With auto-restore, SW and DB are stored on the chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, and a manual clear recovery-mode command is then needed, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the HW. With auto-in-service, SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode. Monitor with show recovery, which reports restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup timestamps, both defaulting to never.

Only if the candidate is empty. rollback must be executed with the commit parameter and optionally a specific commit-id: rollback commit [<commit-id>]; if no commit-id is provided, the most recent commit-record is used. It works both in the Running Datastore, the default, and in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty, which is a way to initialize the candidate. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

show commit retrieves commit record information and lets you visualize the Commit Repository records, but it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither is true on your node there are no records to return. Enable it with set system-policies commit-tracking enabled; note that disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. Syntax is show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>], where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it, and -n selects an exact number of records to obtain. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use set system-policies commit-tracking enabled to turn on the commit-repository feature. With it enabled, all configuration changes done via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records, which can then be visualized, compared and rolled back; disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The values are enabled and disabled, with a default of disabled, so commit tracking is off out of the box. The running datastore is writable by default: the companion writable-running policy also defaults to disabled, and disabling that policy makes it impossible to issue configure commands via the running datastore, forcing use of the candidate. In that state the CLI no longer allows add/set/delete except in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, RESTCONF, gNMI and the WebGUI and TL1 become read-only (gNMI telemetry is still allowed and gNOI is still allowed). Read both with show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running].

The db-passphrase. The system will only accept take-snapshot if the db-passphrase, used for DB snapshot encryption, is configured, either in global configuration as part of security-policies (set security-policies db-passphrase) or locally as a parameter of the command, for example take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters in accordance with the 85-character set known as Z85. Automatic DB snapshots are also not enabled until this parameter is set. Syntax: take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]. db-instance defaults to temp and may be temp, manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is a string 0..128. Access mode is Operational Mode. Taking a snapshot whose name already exists overwrites the existing file.
